name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
strategy: Concentrated long book of five wide-moat, high-ROIC franchises that FUND their own growth out of operating cash flow - V, NVDA, TSM, GOOGL, CME - exiting Meta and halving Alphabet after both turned into negative-free-cash-flow AI-capex borrowers, and adding CME as a wide-moat compounder whose earnings rise with the rate volatility that is the main threat to the rest of the book, against 17% cash at 4%.
reassessment_note: New facts, not drift, drove this. My mandate is net-cash compounders and I had explicitly rebalanced away from second-derivative AI-capex exposure - but research this week shows two of my five holdings have become the capex problem rather than an escape from it. Meta's free cash flow fell 91% year over year to $784M as quarterly capex hit $30.1B (~98% of operating cash flow), buybacks are halted so every vesting grant now dilutes me, and management is weighing a multi-billion equity raise; that is a cash-consuming, dilution-issuing capital story, the opposite of what this book is for, so it goes to zero - and I am selling it at +6.4% into strength rather than after the raise is announced. Alphabet turned free cash flow negative in Q2 2026 for the first time ever with long-term debt doubling to $98B against $175-185B of 2026 capex; it is still a great asset (Cloud +82%, the ad-exchange antitrust win, Gemini distribution), but at 25.5x FORWARD earnings versus 17x trailing the depreciation wave is already visible in estimates, so it drops from my top weight of 24% to a normal 14%. The proceeds go where the cash actually is: NVDA at 19x forward with $120B of net income (+65%) and a record $150B buyback increase taking capacity to $235B is, ironically, now the most shareholder-cash-generative name I own, and TSM at 19.9x forward is compounding operating income +65% on pricing power. V rises to top weight because it is the purest expression of the mandate in this regime - asset-light, ~65% operating margins, no AI capex, and volume linked to nominal spend, which is exactly what rises when the Fed is hiking into sticky inflation. The macro is the second driver: the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00%, the 10-year is above 5.2% and the 30-year is at 2004 highs. Rather than hide in cash, which loses in real terms when inflation is the problem, I bought the volatility itself - CME's rates complex is over half its volume, August ADV was its second-highest ever with Treasury ADV +15%, and it earns interest on member margin deposits, so it gets paid by the same bond rout that would compress my growth multiples. Turnover is ~45% of the book, costing roughly 2bps all-in, which is far too cheap to justify holding a position I no longer believe in.

positions.thesis: Top weight because Visa is the one holding whose economics IMPROVE in the current regime. It is a toll booth on nominal consumer spending, so an inflation the Fed is still hiking against flows straight into payment volume, and with essentially no capital intensity it has no AI-capex hole to fund - it converts nearly all operating profit to cash at ~65% operating margins and keeps buying back stock while Meta and Alphabet cannot. The structural bear case was always disintermediation by stablecoins; this quarter inverted it - Visa now runs 160+ stablecoin-linked card programs with volume up ~200% y/y, stablecoin settlement past a $20B annualized run rate (15x a year ago), and it operates a validator node on Circle's Arc L1, so the supposed disruptor is becoming an additional rail it monetizes. At 25.4x forward for a duopoly with this durability I am happy to size up, and the 14% stop is tight because this is a low-beta name where a 14% drawdown would signal something genuinely broken rather than noise.

Raised from 15% because the buyback authorization resolved my main mandate objection. My book is supposed to own net-cash businesses that return capital, and Nvidia just authorized a record $150B increase to $235B of repurchase capacity on top of $120B of net income (+65%) and $215.9B of revenue (+65%) - it is now the largest capital-returner in the AI complex at the exact moment the hyperscalers halted theirs. Crucially it sits on the RIGHT side of the capex problem: the $602B the hyperscalers are spending in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money, lands in Nvidia's revenue line, so I get the AI exposure through the cash recipient rather than the cash burner. At 19.0x forward against 28.9x trailing it is the cheapest megacap I own on forward earnings, which is the opposite of the long-duration valuation risk a 5.2% ten-year punishes. The risk is that the capex it depends on is being debt-financed into a bond rout, so the 20% stop stays wide enough for its beta but hard enough to cap the loss at ~4% of NAV, and I take profits at +35%.

Held at roughly current size, up one point, because it is the clearest pricing-power compounder in the book: Q2 operating income +65% and net income +77% on revenue growth of ~53%, meaning margins are expanding faster than volumes - the signature of a monopoly raising price, not a cyclical catching a wave. It has an effective monopoly on leading-edge nodes, so every AI accelerator design from every competing customer funnels through the same fabs, which makes it a bet on AI compute demand in aggregate rather than on any one chip winning. Its capex is heavy at $60-64B but unlike Meta's it earns an obvious return, and it is being co-funded by customers and the $265B Arizona buildout. At 19.9x forward it is priced like a cyclical rather than the bottleneck it is. I keep it at 16% rather than larger purely because of the Taiwan-concentration tail risk that no amount of financial quality offsets, and the 20% stop and 30% take-profit reflect a name that gaps on geopolitics.

Cut from my 24% top weight to a normal position, not exited, because the business is excellent and the balance sheet trend is not. Alphabet went free-cash-flow negative in Q2 2026 for the first time in its history while long-term debt more than doubled to $98B against $175-185B of planned 2026 capex - by my mandate's own test it has stopped being a net-cash self-funding compounder, and the market is saying so, with the stock 16% below its $408 high despite a broad tech rally. The forward multiple of 25.5x against a 17.2x trailing multiple is the tell: consensus already expects the depreciation wave from this buildout to eat earnings. I keep a real position because the franchise quality is intact and genuinely improving - Cloud growing 82% y/y, Gemini expanding onto the desktop, TPUs giving it the only vertically integrated silicon stack among the hyperscalers, and a federal judge rejecting the DOJ's push to force divestiture of the ad exchange, which removes the single largest structural overhang. 18% stop.

New position, and the only one bought for what it does when my other four go wrong. CME is a genuine quality compounder on this book's own terms - a regulated near-monopoly exchange with open-interest network effects no competitor has ever dislodged, ~60% operating margins, minimal capital intensity and record H1 2026 revenue, adjusted operating income and EPS - so it belongs here on merit at 22.3x with a 4.3% yield. What makes it the right ADD now is that its revenue driver is the precise shock threatening the rest of the portfolio: the Fed has hiked to 3.75-4.00%, the ten-year is above 5.2% and the thirty-year is at 2004 highs, and interest-rate futures are over half of CME's volume, with August ADV of 29.7M contracts its second-highest ever and Treasury ADV +15% y/y. It is also paid twice by higher rates, earning interest on the enormous member margin deposits it holds. That gives me a rate-volatility hedge that is accretive rather than a cost, which is why I prefer it to simply raising cash to 4% in an inflationary regime. Sized at 11% and stopped at 12% because it is low-beta and a 12% fall would mean the volatility thesis had failed outright.
